svg.title: Profiles & bond energies
svg.desc: Energy is conserved: Exothermic pays energy out to surroundings → surroundings warm; products have less energy. Endothermic takes energy from surroundings → surroundings cool; products have more energy. A starting spark does not make an overall reaction endothermic. Examples & applications: Exothermic: combustion, many oxidation reactions, neutralisation → hand warmers/self-heating cans. Endothermic: thermal decomposition; citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate → cooling applications. Judge temperature, duration, safety, cost and disposal. Profile axes & peak: Energy vertically; reaction progress horizontally. Reactants and products at flat levels joined by curved peak. Activation energy: minimum collision energy; measure reactant level to peak. Overall change is between reactant and product levels. Products decide the sign: Products lower → energy transferred out, negative overall change. Products higher → energy taken in, positive. Activation energy is not measured from the baseline; it is not the overall change. Both exothermic and endothermic reactions need activation energy. Count bonds correctly: Overall = broken − formed. Breaking takes in energy; making releases it. Include equation coefficients. H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Given 436, 243, 431 kJ/mol: break 436 + 243 = 679; form 2 × 431 = 862. 679 − 862 = −183 kJ for molar quantities in equation: exothermic. Unknown bond energy: If H–Cl energy is x and overall change is −183: 679 − 2x = −183. 2x = 862 → x = 431 kJ/mol. Use the data supplied. CH₄ has four C–H bonds; 2H₂O contains four O–H bonds. Do not confuse bonds with molecules.
